references.text: In [ref:5 Mos 13:7|Deuteronomy 13:6], it is warned that even close family members – brother, son, daughter, wife – can lead one into apostasy. Jesus radicalizes this principle: loyalty to him must take precedence over even the closest family ties.

In [ref:5 Mos 33:9|Deuteronomy 33:9], it is said about the tribe of Levi that they said concerning their father and mother, "I have not seen him/her", and they did not acknowledge their brothers or children. This illustrates setting God's call ahead of family loyalty, as Jesus demands of his disciples.

In [ref:Matt 10:37|Matthew 10:37], Jesus says: "Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." This parallels Luke 14:26, where the requirement to "hate" one's family is a Semitic expression meaning to love less by comparison.

[ref:Matt 10:38-39|Matthew 10:38-39] speaks about taking up one's cross and following Jesus, and losing one's life for Jesus' sake. This expands on the final part of Luke 14:26 regarding hating "one's own soul" (one's own life) in order to be a disciple of Jesus.

In [ref:Matt 19:29|Matthew 19:29], Jesus promises that whoever has left house, brothers, sisters, father, mother, children or fields for his name's sake will receive a hundredfold. This shows that leaving family for Jesus' sake comes with a promise attached.

In [ref:Luk 9:23-24|Luke 9:23-24], Jesus calls the disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross daily and follow him. Whoever wants to save their life will lose it. This expands on the requirement in 14:26 to hate one's own life.

[ref:Luk 18:29-30|Luke 18:29-30] repeats the theme: whoever has left house, wife, brothers, parents or children for the sake of God's kingdom will receive many times more. Jesus confirms that discipleship may require leaving family members behind.

In [ref:Joh 12:25|John 12:25], Jesus says: "Whoever loves their life will lose it, and whoever hates their life in this world will keep it for eternal life." The phrase "hate one's life" corresponds directly to the expression in Luke 14:26 about hating one's own soul.

In [ref:Rom 9:13|Romans 9:13], [ref:Mal 1:2-3|Malachi 1:2-3] is quoted: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." Here "hate" is used in a Semitic comparative sense – to prefer one over the other – which clarifies how "hate" in Luke 14:26 should be understood.

In [ref:Fil 3:7-8|Philippians 3:7-8], Paul counts everything he had as loss for Christ's sake and considers all things worthless to gain Christ. This reflects the radical discipleship in Luke 14:26, where everything – even one's own life – must be subordinated to the relationship with Jesus.

[ref:Åp 12:11|Revelation 12:11] describes believers as having overcome the accuser because they "did not love their lives even unto death". This reflects Jesus' requirement in Luke 14:26 to hate one's own life for his sake.
